title: Stories Are Weapons: Psychological Warfare and the American Mind
description:
A history of psychological warfare in the United States and of how its methods moved from foreign campaigns into domestic culture wars, by the journalist and novelist Annalee Newitz.

Newitz begins with Benjamin Franklin's fake newspaper in the Revolutionary War and the nineteenth-century wars on Indigenous nations, and follows the line through the Cold War to online influence campaigns. The book argues that postwar psychological operatives drew on science fiction writing and advertising, and that these tactics now appear in fights over race and intelligence, school boards and LGBT students, and feminism. It closes on researchers and activists working toward what Newitz calls psychological disarmament. Norton published the hardcover on 4 June 2024.

Newitz is a science journalist who also writes fiction, and was the founder of io9 and editor-in-chief of Gizmodo. Earlier nonfiction includes Four Lost Cities and Scatter, Adapt, and Remember. Their novels include Autonomous, The Future of Another Timeline and The Terraformers.

title: Obfuscation: A User's Guide for Privacy and Protest
description:
A handbook for resisting data collection by adding noise to it, written for ordinary users who cannot opt out of surveillance by corporations and governments.

Brunton and Nissenbaum define obfuscation as the deliberate use of ambiguous, confusing or misleading information to interfere with surveillance. They draw on cases from radar chaff dropped by Second World War pilots to Twitter bots that disrupted protest hashtags and software that masks search queries, then ask whether such tactics are justified and how they can be combined with other privacy practices and tools. The MIT Press edition was published in September 2015.

When the book appeared, Finn Brunton taught media, culture and communication at New York University, and Helen Nissenbaum was a professor there and directed its Information Law Institute. Brunton is also the author of Spam: A Shadow History of the Internet.

title: Through the Crosshairs: War, Visual Culture, and the Weaponized Gaze
description:
A study of how footage from weapon-mounted cameras left the battlefield and became a familiar part of civilian screen culture.

Stahl follows gun-camera and targeting imagery through news broadcasts, entertainment, video games and social media. He argues that this view through the crosshairs shapes how the public understands armed conflict and state violence. The book appeared from Rutgers University Press in June 2018 in its War Culture series.

Roger Stahl is an associate professor of communication studies at the University of Georgia. He wrote Militainment, Inc. and has worked on documentary films about the relationship between the military and entertainment industries, including Returning Fire. This book carries that research from entertainment into the imagery of surveillance and targeting.

title: No Place to Hide: Behind the Scenes of Our Emerging Surveillance Society
description:
An investigative account of how private data brokers and government agencies built a shared system for tracking Americans after September 11.

O'Harrow follows companies such as Acxiom, ChoicePoint and Seisint, which hold billions of records on individuals and sell or share them with law enforcement and intelligence agencies. He names the result a "security industrial complex" and describes systems like the Matrix, which joined criminal records to commercial data. He also raises problems of inaccurate data and identity theft. Free Press published the book in 2005.

O'Harrow was a reporter for The Washington Post and a Pulitzer Prize finalist for articles on privacy and technology. He received the 2003 Carnegie Mellon Cyber Security Reporting Award. The book comes from his reporting on privacy and technology.

title: Black Transparency: The Right to Know in the Age of Mass Surveillance
description:
A book-length essay on involuntary disclosure, leaks and whistleblowing, written by a design studio rather than a policy analyst.

Metahaven uses the term black transparency for information that escapes against the will of its keepers, and follows it through international relations, the ethics of whistleblowers and the surveillance of everyday digital life. The book mixes essay and fanzine formats, and ties transparency to design, architecture and popular culture. Sternberg Press published it in October 2015 in its Design series.

Metahaven is Vinca Kruk and Daniel van der Velden, who founded the studio in 2007. Its work includes the visual identity for WikiLeaks and the book Uncorporate Identity (2010).

title: Networks of New York: An Illustrated Field Guide to Urban Internet Infrastructure
description:
A pocket field guide to the physical internet, which Ingrid Burrington locates in the sidewalk markings, manhole covers and buildings of New York.

Burrington uses New York as her reference point and more than fifty color illustrations as her map. She decodes spray-painted sidewalk markings, explains the history behind cryptic manhole covers, and points out subway cameras and carrier hotels. Along the way she covers the NYPD's surveillance apparatus, twentieth-century telecommunication monopolies, high-frequency trading on Wall Street and the downtown building that houses both Google and the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force. Melville House published it in August 2016.

Burrington is a writer and artist based in Brooklyn whose work concerns data, internet infrastructure and the tech industry. She turned to network infrastructure in 2013, following the Snowden revelations. She is a founding member of Deep Lab, and her writing has appeared in The Atlantic and The Nation.

title: Before and After: Documenting the Architecture of Disaster
description:
A short illustrated essay on the before-and-after image as a way of documenting destruction, from its origins to satellite surveillance.

Satellite photography shows the effects of war or climate change from the distance of orbit, but rarely the event itself. Eyal and Ines Weizman argue that an architectural expert is needed to fill that gap with a narrative. They trace the before-and-after image from nineteenth-century Paris to current satellite imagery, in which state militaries monitor civilians and humanitarian organisations monitor the militaries. Interpreting these images is never straightforward, and the essay asks who can see in higher resolution and who controls the size of the pixels. The book runs 70 pages and was published by Strelka Press in 2014.

Eyal Weizman, an architect born in Haifa in 1970, founded the agency Forensic Architecture in 2010 and directs it at Goldsmiths, University of London. His books include Hollow Land (2007) and Forensic Architecture: Violence at the Threshold of Detectability (2017).

title: Can Jokes Bring Down Governments? Memes, Design and Politics
description:
An essay by the Amsterdam design studio Metahaven on how protest works when the stated position of government is that there is no alternative.

The book starts from the question of how one dissents in that situation. It proposes that protest now has new strategies, beginning with the internet meme, and treats jokes as an open-source weapon of politics. The essay addresses the austerity politics of Europe and the forms of resistance against them. It was published by Strelka Press (listed as Strelka Institute), as an 82-page paperback in 2014. The cover is a red silhouette of a cat washing itself.

Metahaven was founded in 2007 by the graphic designers Vinca Kruk and Daniel van der Velden, and describes itself as a strategic graphic design agency. Its work spans publications and digital projects, including the visual identity for WikiLeaks, the Sealand Identity Project and the books Uncorporate Identity (2010) and Black Transparency: The Right to Know in the Age of Mass Surveillance (2015).

title: The Administration of Fear
description:
A book-length interview in which Paul Virilio argues that fear has become an everyday landscape and that states have a stake in managing it.

Virilio describes a world that is itself limited, saturated and manipulated, with stock-market crises, undifferentiated terrorism and lightning pandemics producing a stressful claustrophobia. He argues that globalization has eroded the prerogatives of states, which now have to convince citizens that they can ensure their physical safety, and are tempted to orchestrate fear as policy. The "propaganda of progress" and the illuminism of new technologies supply further vectors for fear by manufacturing frenzy and stupor. Virilio reads the 2007 economic catastrophe as capitalism accelerating, not collapsing. The conversation is with Bertrand Richard and was translated by Ames Hodges. Semiotext(e) published it on 24 February 2012 as number 10 in its Intervention Series.

Virilio (1932-2018) was a French urbanist and theorist best known for dromology, the study of the logic and impact of speed. His other books include Speed and Politics, War and Cinema: The Logistics of Perception, Bunker Archaeology and The Information Bomb.

title: Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes
description:
A foundational analysis of propaganda by the French philosopher Jacques Ellul, who treats it as a permanent condition of technological society and not as an occasional wartime tool.

Ellul approaches propaganda through both psychology and sociology. He sorts its techniques into categories, traces how modern technology carries them through a population, and argues that propaganda is a threat to democratic life. Vintage issued the English-language paperback on 12 January 1973. The Los Angeles Times called it a presentation of propaganda as the most serious threat to humanity in the modern world, and Kirkus Reviews described the analysis as brilliant, thoroughgoing and frightening.

Ellul (1912-1994) taught at the University of Bordeaux and was involved in the French Resistance during the Second World War. He wrote widely on technology and its social effects, and the cover of this edition names The Technological Society as his earlier book. He is also described as a Christian anarchist.

title: Branding Terror: The Logotypes and Iconography of Insurgent Groups and Terrorist Organizations
description:
A reference work that reads terrorist and insurgent organizations as brands, cataloguing the symbols they use to announce themselves.

The book has more than sixty entries. Each gives a short account of a group's ideology, leadership and methods, then analyses its visual identity: the symbolism, colours and typography of its logo and flag. It also carries a chronology of major terrorist actions, a glossary, seven maps and about 150 colour illustrations. The authors state that it makes no political statements, and offer it as counter-intelligence insight and as a resource for graphic designers. Merrell published it in April 2013.

Artur Beifuss formerly worked for the United Nations as a counter-terrorism analyst. Francesco Trivini Bellini is a graphic designer and creative director. Steven Heller, formerly art director at the New York Times, wrote the foreword.

title: Preliminary Materials for a Theory of the Young-Girl
description:
A short theoretical text from Tiqqun that treats the "Young-Girl" as consumer society's model citizen and the figure of total integration into the market.

First published in France in 1999, the book was translated by Ariana Reines for Semiotext(e)'s Intervention Series, where it is number 12, and appeared in English on 22 June 2012 in 144 pages. It argues that the Young-Girl is not always young and is increasingly not female, and follows how youth, sexuality and seduction are bound up with consumption and competition. It draws on Proust's Albertine, Gombrowicz's Ferdydurke and Klossowski's idea of living currency.

Tiqqun was a French journal of anonymous philosophical texts that ran two issues, in February 1999 and October 2001. The first issue named an editorial board that included Julien Coupat, though the names were dropped from the English translations. The journal introduced the figures of the Young-Girl and Bloom, drawing on Debord's spectacle and Foucault's biopower. Related texts in English include Introduction to Civil War, The Cybernetic Hypothesis and Theory of Bloom.

title: The Interventionists: Users' Manual for the Creative Disruption of Everyday Life
contributors: Joseph Thompson (Contributor); Nicholas Mirzoeff (Contributor); C. Ondine Chavoya (Contributor)
description:
A reader and field guide to artistic activism, edited by Nato Thompson and Gregory Sholette and published by MASS MoCA, with the MIT Press distributing.

The book accompanied the exhibition The Interventionists: Art in the Social Sphere, shown at MASS MoCA from May 2004 to March 2005, with 29 artists and collectives and eight new commissions. The show had four sections: Nomads, Reclaim the Streets, Ready to Wear and The Experimental University. Participants included William Pope.L, Lucy Orta, Krzysztof Wodiczko, Michael Rakowitz, Reverend Billy and The Yes Men. The 154-page volume was edited by Thompson and Sholette, with Joseph Thompson, Nicholas Mirzoeff and C. Ondine Chavoya, and designed by Arjen Noordeman.

Nato Thompson organized the show as a curator at MASS MoCA, then became chief curator at Creative Time in 2007, where he organized Living as Form (2011). He wrote Seeing Power (Melville House, 2012). Gregory Sholette is a New York artist and professor at Queens College, CUNY. He co-founded Political Art Documentation/Distribution with Lucy R. Lippard and the group REPOhistory, and wrote Dark Matter (2010).

title: Conspiracist Manifesto
description:
An anonymous political treatise that takes conspiracy seriously as a method of analysis and of resistance, and asks whether the suspicion of critical theory can be told apart from that of conspiracy theory.

The book examines whether capitalism and its social apparatus emerged through conspiratorial design, and argues that the evidence supports this reading. From there it makes the case for coordinated counter-conspiracies as an appropriate strategy at a time when human autonomy is under existential threat. Robert Hurley translated the text, and Semiotext(e) issued it as a 400-page paperback in April 2023. Reviewers in the Chronicle of Higher Education and the Columbia Review read it as a bid to put conspiratorial thinking to political use in an age of misinformation.

The book first appeared in French as Manifeste conspirationniste from Éditions du Seuil in 2022. Its authors say: "This book is anonymous because it belongs to no one." The journalist Thomas Mahler believes, after an investigation, that Julien Coupat and the Invisible Committee wrote it. A French review found it a style before an argument, built on dense references to Foucault, Deleuze and the Situationists.

title: McSweeney's 54: The End of Trust
contributors: Julia Angwin (Contributor); Cory Doctorow (Contributor); Virginia Eubanks (Contributor)
description:
A single-theme issue of McSweeney's that takes distrust, and the data practices behind it, as its subject.

The issue starts from an era of low-level distrust in tech companies, peers, democracy and the justice system, in which no one can be sure who is watching or how the information will be used. It looks at data mining, breaches and misinformation, and at the contradiction of wanting privacy while handing personal information to social platforms. More than thirty writers and experts contribute, among them Julia Angwin, Cory Doctorow and Virginia Eubanks. The hardcover came out on 20 November 2018.

The issue was produced with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which acted as special advisor and helped compile the content. Cindy Cohn, Soraya Okuda, Cory Doctorow, Dave Maass and Bruce Schneier wrote pieces for it. It was McSweeney's first all-nonfiction issue, a break from the short fiction the quarterly usually carries, with essays, debates, interviews, graphs and manifestos. Dave Eggers and Nyuol Lueth Tong edited it. The digital content was released under a Creative Commons license.

title: T.A.Z.: The Temporary Autonomous Zone, Ontological Anarchy, Poetic Terrorism
description:
Hakim Bey's T.A.Z. proposes the temporary autonomous zone, a short-lived space that slips past formal structures of control, as a tactic for anarchist thought and action.

The book has three parts: “Chaos: The Broadsheets of Ontological Anarchism”, “Communiques of the Association for Ontological Anarchy” and the title essay. That essay is divided into sections on pirate utopias, revolutionary waiting, everyday psychotopology, information networks, musical organization and strategies of resistance. Autonomedia published it in 1991 as part of its New Autonomy Series.

Hakim Bey is the pen name of Peter Lamborn Wilson, an anarchist author and poet. Bey later conceded that some autonomous spaces turn out to be less than temporary, and he returned to the idea in Permanent TAZs (1994). The book was reissued by Autonomedia in 2003 and by Pacific Publishing Studio in 2011, and it has been influential in post-left anarchist thought.

title: Uneasy Listening: Notes on Hearing and Being Heard
description:
A short dialogue between a psychoanalyst and a violin maker on what it means to listen and to be heard.

Anouchka Grose and Robert Brewer Young begin as strangers. Their exchange draws on psychoanalytic theory, philosophy and contemporary culture, with each interrupting and unsettling the other as they try to say what listening means. MACK published the paperback, which has a flap and 96 pages, in June 2022 as part of DISCOURSE, a series of small books in which a writer, theorist or artist enters an extended dialogue with a theme, an idea or another person.

Grose is a psychoanalyst and writer practicing in London and the author of two novels and six non-fiction books. Young trained as a luthier in the artists’ studios of Carnegie Hall in New York, lectures in philosophy at the European Graduate School and heads the Scientific Research Department at J&A Beare, London.

title: How to Disappear in America
description:
Seth Price's How to Disappear in America is an artist's book that works as a handbook of evasion, assembled entirely from information found on the internet.

It was published in 2008 as the catalogue for Price's exhibition at Friedrich Petzel Gallery. The book takes the form of the 1960s countercultural manuals that gave instructions for dropping out of mainstream society. Its advice concerns the practical side of using current technology and avoiding capture by law enforcement. The first printing is a sewn hardcover in a dust jacket, offset printed, 95 pages.

The Leopard Press, New York, issued the book, and it has been reprinted at least twice since 2008. Petzel Gallery lists a later hardcover printing under a different ISBN with a red cover and 96 pages.

Drone is the first volume of Unmanned. Architecture and Security Series, a research and publishing project on architecture's role in building contemporary security regimes.

The book gathers researchers from different disciplines whose work seeks to understand and represent the nature and extent of drone operations. It examines how drone technology, cultural production, surveillance and violence bear on one another, and how these developments affect life in cities. title: Monitoring Control
contributors: Bruce Sterling (Text); Christian Marazzi (Conversation); Marco Scotini (Conversation)
description:
A collection of ten texts by the artist and hacktivist Paolo Cirio on surveillance, social media and algorithmic control, published for his 2021 solo exhibition in Modena.

The book adds a text by Bruce Sterling and a conversation between Christian Marazzi, Marco Scotini and Cirio. A gallery of images drawn from the thousands of algorithm patents Cirio has collected online shows the tools used for surveillance and social manipulation. Its subjects include Instagram, Facebook, mugshot websites and Google Street View, and the ways these tools shape daily life. It accompanied the exhibition Monitoring Control at the Palazzina dei Giardini of Fondazione Modena Arti Visive, curated by Marco Scotini and on view from November 2021 to January 2022.

Cirio has spent about twenty years examining the relation between the information society and global capitalism, an approach he calls Evidentiary Realism. The exhibition gathered ten years of his work, among it Street Ghosts, Face to Facebook, Overexposed and Obscurity, and opened with a large new installation, Iris.

title: The Screwball Asses
description:
A 1973 French treatise on homosexual desire and the gay-liberation movement, long misattributed to Guy Hocquenghem and restored here to its author, Christian Maurel.

It first appeared anonymously in the "Three Billion Perverts" issue of Félix Guattari's journal Recherches, which French authorities banned on release. Maurel takes on the militant delusions and internal contradictions of the gay-liberation movement as well as the mores of bourgeois capitalism. He rejects any "pure theory" of homosexuality that would treat its otherness as revolutionary, and argues that the ruling classes invented homosexuality as a sexual ghetto. There are thousands of sexes, he says, but only one sexual desire. This second edition keeps Noura Wedell's English translation, first published in 2009 under Hocquenghem's name, and adds a preface by Hocquenghem's biographer Antoine Idier on the differing positions inside the Front Homosexuel d'Action Révolutionnaire.

Maurel is a writer, journalist and activist. The book is number 3 in the Semiotext(e) Intervention series.

title: Training for the Future Handbook
description:
A handbook of the Training for the Future camps, in which audiences become trainees who pre-enact alternative futures and reclaim the means of production of the future.

It gathers training manuals, interviews and documentation from the camps held between 2018 and 2021. One of them ran at the Ruhrtriennale in Bochum in September 2019, with a faculty of futurologists, hackers, activists and theatre makers who each offered exercises in answering present-day crises. Contributors include Public Movement, Women on Waves, Not An Alternative, Irational, Army of Love and the Laboratory of Insurrectionary Imagination. Remco van Bladel designed the book, which has 320 pages with 118 black-and-white and 86 colour illustrations.

Jonas Staal is a visual artist whose work deals with art, propaganda and democracy. He founded New World Summit and wrote Propaganda Art in the 21st Century. Florian Malzacher is a performing-arts curator, dramaturge and writer, and the author of Truth Is Concrete. The two co-direct the camp.

title: Steal This Book
contributors: Izak Haber (Co-conspirator); Bert Cohen (Accessory after the fact); Lisa Fithian (Foreword); Al Giordano (Introduction)
description:
Abbie Hoffman's 1971 manual for surviving outside the system, a radical guide to getting by without money, permission or an address.

Hoffman began writing it in 1970 in Cook County jail, awaiting the Chicago Seven trial. The book is split into three sections, Survive!, Fight! and Liberate!, and lists ways to get free food, clothing, housing, transportation, medical care and communication, and how to run a guerrilla movement. The final pages give specifics for New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and San Francisco, and a list of other books worth stealing. It was first issued under the Pirate Editions label and distributed by Grove Press, expanding an earlier privately published pamphlet, Fuck the System (1967). This printing carries a foreword by Lisa Fithian and an introduction by Al Giordano.

Hoffman was a political theatre artist and activist. Steal This Book followed Revolution for the Hell of It and Woodstock Nation, and its title and instructions drew scandal on publication.

title: How to Be a Dissident
description:
A short, argued guide to dissent that asks what the people who refused authoritarian conformity had in common, and what an ordinary reader can borrow from them.

Beckerman moves from Socrates to Ai Weiwei and pulls ten qualities out of the lives he examines, including pessimism, humor and recklessness. The book combines intellectual history, biography and cultural analysis, and addresses how integrity is kept up under modern pressures to conform. It runs 208 pages in a pocket-sized trade paperback published by Crown in April 2026.

A collection of projects and essays on architects and designers who leave office practice to build mobile, self-initiated interventions in the city.

The book maps a movement organized around place-making, occupying and squatting, and alternative economies. Its interventions are ecological or technological in scope, all of them mobile, and nearly all were made without permission from city planners. It presents international projects by emerging designers. It asks what architectural permanence is for. It also asks which social, ecological and ethical questions urban planning leaves out. Essays by Mimi Zeiger, Kim Dovey, Alan Smart, Nick Green, Fiona Shipwright and Michael Maginness sit alongside the projects. Featured practitioners include Melissa Jin, Ahmad S Khouja, Kaegh Allen, Edwina Portocarrero and Office of Urban Play.
